question: On which HF and/or MF amateur bands are there portions where General class licensees cannot transmit?
explanation: General class HF privileges are subdivided on 80m, 40m, 20m, and 15m: each has a slice reserved exclusively for Advanced/Amateur Extra licensees (e.g. 7.125-7.175 MHz on 40m, 3.600-3.800 MHz on 80m), so General cannot transmit there. The WARC bands (60m, 30m, 17m, 12m) and 160m/10m have no such Extra-exclusive carve-out under 97.301(d) - General gets the whole band (subject to the usual mode/power rules) - which is why C, not A, B, or D, is the set of bands with a General-excluded portion.

question: On which of the following bands is phone operation prohibited?
explanation: 30 meters (10.100-10.150 MHz) is CW/data-only under the 97.305(c) emission table - no phone (voice) is authorized there for any license class, because the band is shared with fixed and other non-amateur services on terms that don't accommodate voice bandwidth. 160m, 17m, and 12m all have phone privileges somewhere in the band, so they don't fit the question.

question: On which of the following bands is image transmission prohibited?
explanation: Image emissions (SSTV, fax, etc.) share the same restriction as phone on 30 meters - the band is CW/data only per 97.305, with no image authorization anywhere in it. 160m and 12m both permit image transmission, and 20m's phone segment explicitly allows image modes like SSTV, so only 30m fits.

question: On which of the following frequencies are General class licensees prohibited from operating as control operator?
explanation: 7.125-7.175 MHz sits in the gap between General's 40m CW/data privilege (7.025-7.125 MHz) and General's 40m phone privilege (7.175-7.300 MHz) - it's the Advanced/Extra-exclusive slice, so a General control operator may not transmit there at all, matching 97.301(d). By contrast, 28.000-28.025 MHz is inside General's 10m CW/data segment (28.000-28.300 MHz) and 21.275-21.300 MHz is inside General's 15m phone segment (21.275-21.450 MHz) - both are fully authorized to General, so 'all of the above' is wrong.

question: Which of the following applies when the FCC rules designate the amateur service as a secondary user on a band?
answers: Amateur stations must record the call sign of the primary service station before operating on a frequency assigned to that station
Amateur stations may use the band only during emergencies
Amateur stations must not cause harmful interference to primary users and must accept interference from primary users
Amateur stations may only operate during specific hours of the day, while primary users are permitted 24-hour use of the band
explanation: 97.303 sets the basic secondary-user obligation: a station operating on a band where the amateur service is secondary must not cause harmful interference to the primary service and must accept any interference the primary service causes back. There's no rule requiring amateurs to log the primary station's call sign, restricting secondary use to emergencies, or granting the primary service exclusive 24-hour use while amateurs get scraps - those are all invented restrictions not found in Part 97.

question: On which amateur frequencies in the 10-meter band may stations with a General class control operator transmit CW emissions?
explanation: 97.305(a) authorizes CW on any frequency the control operator is authorized to use, and General's 10m authorization runs the entire band, 28.000-29.700 MHz. So even though General's phone/image privilege is limited to 28.300-29.700 MHz and RTTY/data to 28.000-28.300 MHz, CW is not similarly boxed in - it's allowed everywhere General can transmit on 10m, making 'the entire band' correct rather than any of the narrower mode-specific sub-ranges.

question: Which HF bands have segments exclusively allocated to Amateur Extra licensees?
answers: All HF bands except 160 meters and 10 meters
explanation: 80m, 40m, 20m, and 15m each carry a segment reserved exclusively for Advanced/Amateur Extra licensees (same segments referenced in G1A01/G1A05) under 97.301(b)/(d). The WARC bands - 60m, 30m, 17m, 12m - simply have no Extra-exclusive carve-out anywhere in 97.301's band table, so General gets full access there just like Extra does; that rules out both 'all HF bands' and 'all except 160/10m.'

question: Which of the following frequencies is within the General class portion of the 15-meter band?
explanation: 21300 kHz (21.300 MHz) is the only one of the four choices that actually falls in the 15-meter band (21.000-21.450 MHz) at all, and it lands within General's 15m phone segment (21.275-21.450 MHz) per 97.301(d). 14250 kHz is on 20m, 18155 kHz is on 17m, and 24900 kHz is on 12m - all wrong bands entirely, not just wrong license-class segments.

question: What portion of the 10-meter band is available for repeater use?
answers: The portion between 28.1 MHz and 28.2 MHz
The portion between 28.3 MHz and 28.5 MHz
explanation: 97.205(b) lists the frequency segments repeaters may NOT use, and on 10 meters that exclusion is 28.0-29.5 MHz - so the only part of the 10m band (28.0-29.7 MHz) left open for repeater operation is 29.5-29.7 MHz, the portion above 29.5 MHz. The entire band and the two mid-band ranges offered as distractors both fall inside the excluded 28.0-29.5 MHz zone.

question: When General class licensees are not permitted to use the entire voice portion of a band, which portion of the voice segment is available to them?
answers: The lower frequency portion on frequencies below 7.3 MHz, and the upper portion on frequencies above 14.150 MHz
The upper frequency portion on frequencies below 7.3 MHz, and the lower portion on frequencies above 14.150 MHz
explanation: Wherever General doesn't get the whole voice segment of a shared band, the rule (97.301) consistently gives General the upper part: e.g. 80m phone 3.800-4.000 (upper part of the shared 3.600-4.000 range), 40m phone 7.175-7.300, 20m phone 14.225-14.350, and 15m phone 21.275-21.450 - all the top end of their respective phone allocations, with Advanced/Extra holding the lower part. That consistent pattern is why 'the upper frequency portion' is correct rather than the more complicated split-by-frequency answers.

question: What is the maximum height above ground for an antenna structure not near a public use airport without requiring notification to the FAA and registration with the FCC?
explanation: 97.15(a) sets the FAA-notification/FCC-registration (Part 17) trigger at structures more than 60.96 meters (200 feet) above ground level - below that height, and away from airport proximity (which triggers separate obstruction-evaluation rules regardless of height), no notification or registration is required. 50 and 100 feet are both well under the real threshold, and 250 feet is above it, so only 200 feet matches the actual rule.

question: With which of the following conditions must beacon stations comply?
answers: No more than one beacon station may transmit in the same band from the same station location
The frequency must be coordinated with the National Beacon Organization
The frequency must be posted on the internet or published in a national periodical
explanation: 97.203(b) is narrow and specific: a station may not run more than one beacon concurrently on the same band from the same location. There's no FCC-recognized 'National Beacon Organization' that coordinates frequencies (that's a fabricated body - international HF propagation beacons are coordinated informally through IARU/NCDXF, not by FCC rule), and there's no requirement to publish a beacon's frequency online or in print, so 'all these choices' is wrong.

question: Which of the following is a purpose of a beacon station as identified in the FCC rules?
answers: Transmission of bulletins of general interest to amateur radio licensees
explanation: 97.3(a)(9) defines a beacon specifically as a station transmitting for observation of propagation and reception (or other related experimental activities) - that's its defining regulatory purpose. Automatic repeater identification and bulletin transmission are real, separate authorized activities under other rules (97.119 and 97.111(b)(6) respectively), but they aren't what makes a station a 'beacon' by definition, so 'all these choices' overstates it.

question: Which of the following transmissions is permitted for all amateur stations?
answers: Unidentified transmissions of less than 10 seconds duration for test purposes only
Automatic retransmission of other amateur signals by any amateur station
Occasional retransmission of weather and propagation forecast information from US government stations
Encrypted messages, if not intended to facilitate a criminal act
explanation: 97.113(c) specifically carves out an exception letting amateur stations occasionally retransmit weather and propagation forecast information originated by US government stations, as an incident of normal operation - not on a regular/scheduled basis. Automatic retransmission of other amateurs' signals is restricted to specifically authorized station types (like repeaters and auxiliary stations), not 'any' station; unidentified test transmissions aren't blanket-exempted by an invented 10-second rule; and 97.113(a)(4) bars messages encoded to obscure their meaning with no 'unless it's not for a crime' exception.

question: Which of the following one-way transmissions are permitted?
answers: Unidentified test transmissions of less than 10 seconds in duration
Transmissions to assist with learning the International Morse code
Regular transmissions offering equipment for sale, if intended for amateur radio use
explanation: The permitted one-way transmission that fits here is transmissions to assist someone learning Morse code, which is listed among the 97.111(b) one-way exceptions (this question's citation as printed, '97.111((5)(b)', is a garbled version of the real cite 97.111(b)(5) - stray extra parenthesis and reversed order, but the rule content is real). Unidentified sub-10-second test transmissions aren't blanket-permitted the way the distractor implies, and 'regular' transmissions advertising equipment for sale - even ham gear - cross into prohibited broadcasting/pecuniary-interest territory under 97.113, so they aren't allowed as routine one-way traffic.

question: Under what conditions are state and local governments permitted to regulate amateur radio antenna structures?
answers: Under no circumstances, FCC rules take priority
At any time and to any extent necessary to accomplish a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity, provided that proper filings are made with the FCC
Only when such structures exceed 50 feet in height and are clearly visible 1,000 feet from the structure
Amateur Service communications must be reasonably accommodated, and regulations must constitute the minimum practical to accommodate a legitimate purpose of the state or local entity
explanation: This is the PRB-1 standard, codified at 97.15(b) from the FCC's 1985 declaratory ruling (101 FCC 2d 952): state and local governments may regulate antenna structures, but their regulation 'must reasonably accommodate amateur service communications and must constitute the minimum practicable regulation to accomplish the [local government's] legitimate purpose.' That's a real but limited power - not 'no regulation ever' (A), not unlimited local authority as long as paperwork is filed with the FCC (B, which invents an FCC filing step that doesn't exist), and not a bright-line height/visibility test (C, which PRB-1 doesn't set).

question: What are the restrictions on the use of abbreviations or procedural signals in the amateur service?
answers: They may be used if they do not obscure the meaning of a message
They are limited to those expressly listed in Part 97 of the FCC rules
explanation: 97.113(a)(4) prohibits messages 'encoded for the purpose of obscuring their meaning' - the flip side of that rule is that abbreviations and procedural signals (Q signals, prosigns, common shorthand) are fine as long as they don't hide what's being said. There's no rule limiting hams to Q signals only, no rule banning abbreviations outright, and Part 97 doesn't publish an exhaustive approved list - the standard is about intent/effect (obscuring meaning), not a fixed vocabulary.

question: When is it permissible to communicate with amateur stations in countries outside the areas administered by the Federal Communications Commission?
answers: Only when the foreign country has a formal third-party agreement filed with the FCC
When the contact is with amateurs in any country except those whose administrations have notified the ITU that they object to such communications
Only when the contact is with amateurs licensed by a country which is a member of the United Nations, or by a territory possessed by such a country
Only when the contact is with amateurs licensed by a country which is a member of the International Amateur Radio Union, or by a territory possessed by such a country
explanation: 97.111(a)(1) permits contact with amateur stations in any country except those whose administration has formally notified the ITU that it objects to such communications - a short, published exclusion list, not an opt-in system. There's no requirement for a filed third-party agreement just to make basic two-way contact (that requirement applies specifically to relaying third-party traffic, a different rule), and there's no UN-membership or IARU-membership gate on who a US ham may talk to.

question: On what HF frequencies are automatically controlled beacons permitted?
answers: On any frequency if power is less than 1 watt
On any frequency if transmissions are in Morse code
explanation: 97.203(d) lists the specific HF/VHF/UHF segments where a beacon may run under automatic control, and on HF that's 28.20-28.30 MHz (the rest of the list is VHF/UHF: 50.06-50.08, 144.275-144.300, 222.05-222.06, and 432.300-432.400 MHz, plus all bands 33cm and shorter). There's no blanket 'any frequency if under 1 watt' or 'any frequency if CW' exception, and 21.08-21.09 MHz isn't on the authorized list at all.

question: What is the power limit for beacon stations?
explanation: 97.203(c) caps beacon transmitter power at 100 watts PEP output - a deliberately modest limit since a beacon's job (propagation observation) doesn't require high power, and it minimizes the beacon's footprint as an unattended, continuously-transmitting station. 10W and 20W are both below the actual cap, and 200W exceeds it.

question: Who or what determines “good engineering and good amateur practice,” as applied to the operation of an amateur station in all respects not covered by the Part 97 rules?
explanation: 97.101(a) itself states that in all respects not specifically covered by the rules, a station must be operated per 'good engineering and good amateur practice' - and since that standard is written into an FCC rule, it's the FCC's rule that ultimately governs the requirement (the FCC evaluates and enforces it, even though it's an intentionally flexible, non-numeric standard). The control operator applies good practice day-to-day, but doesn't get to unilaterally define what counts; IEEE and ITU are not the regulatory bodies with authority here.

question: What is the maximum transmitter power an amateur station may use on 10.140 MHz?
explanation: 97.313(c)(1) caps power at 200 watts PEP output on the 30-meter band (10.100-10.150 MHz, which includes 10.140 MHz) - and unlike most Part 97 power sub-limits, this one applies to every license class, not just Novice/Technician, because 30m is shared with non-amateur fixed-service allocations under terms that require the lower power everywhere on the band. 1000W, 1500W, and 2000W are all above that hard cap.

question: What is the maximum transmitter power an amateur station may use on the 12-meter band?
answers: An effective radiated power equivalent to 100 watts from a half-wave dipole
explanation: 12 meters carries none of the special reduced-power restrictions that apply to bands like 30m, 60m, 630m, or 2200m, so it falls under the general Part 97 ceiling of 1500 watts PEP output (97.313). 50W and 200W are both well under the real limit, and 'ERP equivalent to 100W from a dipole' is the 60-meter band's power definition (97.313(i)/(j)), not 12-meter's.

question: What is the maximum bandwidth permitted by FCC rules for amateur radio stations transmitting on USB frequencies in the 60-meter band?
explanation: 97.303(h)(1) sets the maximum occupied bandwidth on 60-meter USB transmissions at 2.8 kHz - consistent with a standard SSB voice channel width, and tight enough to fit the band's narrow, channelized allocation without splattering onto adjacent users who share the spectrum. 5.6 kHz is roughly double the real limit, and 1.8/3 kHz are both off the actual codified number.

question: Which of the following is required by the FCC rules when operating in the 60-meter band?
answers: If you are using an antenna other than a dipole, you must keep a record of the gain of your antenna
You must keep a record of the date, time, frequency, power level, and stations worked
You must keep a record of all third-party traffic
You must keep a record of the manufacturer of your equipment and the antenna used
explanation: 97.303(i) defines the 60-meter power limit as an effective radiated power of 100 watts relative to a dipole - so if you're running an antenna with gain over a dipole, you have to back off transmitter power to stay under that ERP cap, and the rule requires keeping a record of that antenna's gain to document you did so. It doesn't require logging every contact's date/time/power/station (routine but not mandated for this purpose), logging third-party traffic (a different topic entirely), or recording equipment manufacturer info.

question: What is the limit for transmitter power on the 28 MHz band for a General Class control operator?
explanation: 10 meters (28 MHz) has no special reduced-power carve-out for General, so the ordinary Part 97 ceiling applies: 1500 watts PEP output (97.313). 100W, 1000W, and 2000W are all off that mark - 2000W in particular exceeds what any amateur station, regardless of class, is ever allowed to run.

question: What is the limit for transmitter power on the 1.8 MHz band?
explanation: 1.8 MHz is on 160 meters, which also has no special reduced-power restriction, so the same general 1500-watt PEP ceiling from 97.313 applies. 200W, 1000W, and 1200W all understate the actual limit.

question: What must be done before using a new digital protocol on the air?
answers: Obtain an experimental license from the FCC
Publicly document the technical characteristics of the protocol
Submit a rule-making proposal to the FCC describing the codes and methods of the technique
explanation: 97.309(a)(4) lets amateurs use RTTY/data techniques beyond the three explicitly named codes (Baudot, AMTOR, ASCII) as long as the technique's technical characteristics have been documented publicly - that's literally how modes like PACTOR, CLOVER, G-TOR, and newer digital protocols became legal to use, by publishing how they work rather than by getting FCC pre-approval. There's no FCC type-certification process, no experimental-license requirement, and no rulemaking-proposal step for an individual station to start using a new mode.

question: What measurement is specified by FCC rules that regulate maximum power?
explanation: 97.313's power limits, and the PEP definition in 97.3, are both specified as peak envelope power measured at the transmitter's output - not at the antenna (which would include feed-line loss/gain and vary station to station) and not as an RMS figure (PEP and RMS measure different things for a modulated signal). So 'PEP output from the transmitter' is the only choice matching how Part 97 actually defines the measurement point.

question: Who may receive partial credit for the elements represented by an expired amateur radio license?
answers: Any person who can demonstrate that they once held an FCC-issued General, Advanced, or Amateur Extra class license that was not revoked by the FCC
Anyone who held an FCC-issued amateur radio license that expired not less than 5 and not more than 15 years ago
Any person who previously held an amateur license issued by another country, but only if that country has a current reciprocal licensing agreement with the FCC
Only persons who once held an FCC issued Novice, Technician, or Technician Plus license
explanation: 97.501/97.505(a) give partial exam-element credit to anyone who can show they once held an FCC-issued General, Advanced, or Amateur Extra license that wasn't revoked - there's no minimum/maximum number of years since expiration (ruling out the '5 to 15 years' distractor), no dependency on a foreign reciprocal agreement (that's unrelated to crediting a US license), and Novice/Technician/Technician Plus licenses don't carry Element 3 credit the way General-and-above licenses do, so that distractor is backwards.

question: What license examinations may you administer as an accredited Volunteer Examiner holding a General class operator license?
answers: None, only Amateur Extra class licensees may be accredited
explanation: 97.509(b)(3)(i) sets the license-class floor for administering each exam level: Amateur Extra, Advanced, or General may administer a Technician exam; Amateur Extra or Advanced may administer a General exam; only Amateur Extra may administer an Amateur Extra exam. So a General-class VE - even though they personally hold General privileges - can only administer Technician exams, one tier below their own license, not General or Extra exams.

question: On which of the following band segments may you operate if you are a Technician class operator and have an unexpired Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE) for General class privileges?
answers: Only the Technician band segments until your upgrade is posted in the FCC database
Only on the Technician band segments until you have a receipt for the FCC application fee payment
On any General or Technician class band segment
On any General or Technician class band segment except 30 meters and 60 meters
explanation: 97.9(b) gives a licensee holding an unexpired CSCE for a higher class immediate, full operating privileges of that higher class - on any General or Technician band segment - while the paperwork is still pending, with no need to wait for the FCC database to show the upgrade or for a fee-payment receipt. There's also no carve-out excluding 30m/60m from that provisional privilege.

question: Who must observe the administration of a Technician class license examination?
answers: At least three Volunteer Examiners of General class or higher
At least two Volunteer Examiners of General class or higher
At least two Volunteer Examiners of Technician class or higher
At least three Volunteer Examiners of Technician class
explanation: The real requirement combines two subsections of 97.509: (a) requires a team of at least 3 VEs to administer any amateur exam, and (b)(3)(i) requires each of those VEs to hold at least a General class license to administer a Technician exam - together, 'at least three VEs of General class or higher.' The printed citation for this question, '97.509(3)(i)(c)', is a malformed/garbled version of that - it's missing the leading '(b)' before '(3)(i)' and the trailing '(c)' doesn't fit (97.509(c) is actually about observing the candidate throughout the exam, unrelated to the team-size requirement), but the substance above is accurate.

question: When operating a US station by remote control from outside the country, what license is required of the control operator?
answers: Only an appropriate US operator/primary license and a special remote station permit from the FCC
Only a license from the foreign country, as long as the call sign includes identification of portable operation in the US
A license from the foreign country and a special remote station permit from the FCC
explanation: 97.7 requires every transmitting amateur station to have a control operator holding a valid amateur operator/primary station license - being physically located outside the US when remotely controlling a US station doesn't change that requirement or substitute a foreign license for it. There's no such thing as a 'special remote station permit' in Part 97, so both B and D describe a nonexistent credential.

question: Until an upgrade to General class is shown in the FCC database, when must a Technician licensee identify with “AG” after their call sign?
answers: Whenever they operate using General class frequency privileges
Whenever they operate on any amateur frequency
Whenever they operate using Technician frequency privileges
A special identifier is not required if their General class license application has been filed with the FCC
explanation: 97.119(f)(2) requires the 'AG' identifier specifically when the Technician-class operator is exercising General class privileges under an unexpired CSCE - not on every transmission regardless of what privileges are being used. If they're just operating on ordinary Technician segments, no special suffix is needed since nothing elevated is happening, and the requirement runs until the upgrade actually appears in the FCC database - simply having filed the application isn't enough to drop the requirement.

question: Volunteer Examiners are accredited by what organization?
explanation: 97.509(b)(1) requires each VE to be accredited by a Volunteer Examiner Coordinator (VEC) - a body the FCC certifies to run the accreditation program, but the FCC itself doesn't directly accredit individual VEs. The Universal Licensing System is just the FCC's online license database, and the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau is an FCC organizational unit, not an accrediting body - neither performs VE accreditation.

question: Which of the following criteria must be met for a non-US citizen to be an accredited Volunteer Examiner?
answers: The person must be a resident of the US for a minimum of 5 years
The person must hold an FCC granted amateur radio license of General class or above
The person’s home citizenship must be in ITU region 2
None of these choices is correct; a non-US citizen cannot be a Volunteer Examiner
explanation: 97.509(b)(3) ties VE eligibility to holding an FCC-granted amateur operator license of General class or above - citizenship isn't the gating factor at all, so a non-US citizen can be an accredited VE as long as they hold that FCC license. There's no 5-year US-residency requirement and no rule tying eligibility to an operator's home country being in ITU Region 2, and 'a non-US citizen cannot be a VE' is simply false.

question: How long is a Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE) valid for exam element credit?
answers: For as long as your current license is valid
explanation: 97.9(b) (with the mechanics spelled out in 97.505(b)) gives a CSCE 365 days of validity for element credit - a full year from the date the examinee passed the element(s) it documents. 30 and 180 days both undercut that, and 'as long as your license is valid' describes something else (the license term itself, which is a separate 10-year renewal cycle, not the CSCE's credit window).

question: What is the minimum age that one must be to qualify as an accredited Volunteer Examiner?
explanation: 97.509(b)(2) sets the minimum VE age at 18 years - a hard floor with no exceptions listed in the rule. 16 and 21 both miss the actual number, and there is in fact an age limit, so 'no age limit' is wrong.

question: What action is required to obtain a new General class license after a previously held license has expired and the two-year grace period has passed?
answers: They must have a letter from the FCC showing they once held an amateur or commercial license
There are no requirements other than being able to show a copy of the expired license
Contact the FCC to have the license reinstated
The applicant must show proof of the appropriate expired license grant and pass the current Element 2 exam
explanation: Once the two-year renewal grace period has run out, 97.505's element-credit framework still lets an applicant claim credit for the written elements the old grant represented (Element 3 for a General, plus Element 4 if it was Advanced or Extra), but 97.501 requires passing a live exam for any new license grant - so in practice the applicant has to document the old license and then sit (and pass) the current Element 2 written exam to get the new grant. Just having a copy of the old license, or a letter proving past licensure, isn't enough by itself, and the FCC doesn't administratively 'reinstate' an expired license once the grace period is gone.

question: When operating a station in South America by remote control over the internet from the US, what regulations apply?
answers: Those of both the remote station’s country and the FCC
Those of the remote station’s country and the FCC’s third-party regulations
Only those of the remote station’s country
explanation: The governing principle here is jurisdictional: a transmitter is subject to the telecommunications law of the country where it's physically located, not the operator's home country or the FCC's authority, which under 97.5 extends only to stations within the US/its territories or aboard US-registered vessels and craft - none of which describes a station physically sited in South America. So only that country's own regulations apply, regardless of the fact the operator is controlling it remotely from the US over the internet. Flagging a citation problem: the ref printed for this question, 97.507, is actually the VE-program rule on 'Preparing an examination' (who may write exam question sets) and has nothing to do with jurisdiction over a remote-controlled foreign station - this looks like a copy/paste error carried in the official NCVEC pool document itself, not something specific to this app's data.

question: Which of the following would disqualify a third party from participating in sending a message via an amateur station?
answers: The third party’s amateur license has been revoked and not reinstated
The third party is not a US citizen
The third party is speaking in a language other than English
explanation: 97.115(b)(2) disqualifies a third party whose amateur license has been revoked and not since reinstated (also covered: an active suspension, or surrendering a license mid-revocation/suspension proceeding). Being a non-US citizen or speaking a language other than English aren't disqualifiers under this rule - many third-party arrangements exist precisely to let non-hams and people who don't speak English participate as third parties, so 'all these choices' overreaches.

question: When may a 10-meter repeater retransmit the 2-meter signal from a station that has a Technician class control operator?
answers: Only if the station on 10-meters is operating under a Special Temporary Authorization allowing such retransmission
Only during an FCC-declared general state of communications emergency
Only if the 10-meter repeater control operator holds at least a General class license
explanation: A repeater operates under the privileges of whatever class its own control operator holds (97.301/97.205(a)), and Technician class has no phone/repeater privilege on 10 meters at all (only a limited CW/data segment). So for a 10m repeater to lawfully retransmit a signal relayed in from 2 meters - regardless of the originating station's Technician-class control operator - the 10m repeater's own control operator has to hold at least General class to be authorized on that part of 10m in the first place. There's no Special Temporary Authorization or emergency-declaration mechanism that substitutes for that.

question: What is required to conduct communications with a digital station operating under automatic control outside the automatic control band segments?
answers: The station initiating the contact must be under local or remote control
The interrogating transmission must be made by another automatically controlled station
No third-party traffic may be transmitted
The control operator of the interrogating station must hold an Amateur Extra class license
explanation: 97.221 requires that, outside the designated automatic-control band segments, an automatically controlled digital station can only respond when interrogated by a station under local or remote control - i.e. a human-supervised station has to be the one initiating contact with it. The distractor in B inverts this (claiming the interrogator must itself be automatic), which is backwards from the actual rule's intent of keeping a person in the loop.

question: Which of the following conditions require a licensed amateur radio operator to take specific steps to avoid harmful interference to other users or facilities?
answers: When operating within one mile of an FCC Monitoring Station
When using a band where the Amateur Service is secondary
When a station is transmitting spread spectrum emissions
explanation: All three listed conditions independently trigger their own interference-avoidance duty: 97.13(b) requires protecting an FCC monitoring facility from harmful interference within 1 mile of it, 97.303 requires a secondary-service station to avoid harmful interference to (and accept interference from) the primary service, and 97.311(b) requires a spread-spectrum station to avoid harmful interference to other authorized emissions while accepting interference from them. Since none of these obligations substitutes for the others, 'all these choices' is correct.

question: What are the restrictions on messages sent to a third party in a country with which there is a Third-Party Agreement?
answers: They must relate to emergencies or disaster relief
They must be for other licensed amateurs
They must relate to amateur radio, or remarks of a personal character, or messages relating to emergencies or disaster relief
The message must be limited to no longer than 1 minute in duration and the name of the third party must be recorded in the station log
explanation: Two rules combine here: 97.117 limits transmissions to a foreign country to matters incidental to the amateur service and remarks of a personal character, and 97.115(a)(2) separately permits third-party traffic related to emergencies or disaster relief even where a general Third-Party Agreement wouldn't otherwise cover the content. Together that produces the broader 'amateur-related, personal, or emergency/disaster-relief' answer - it's not limited to emergencies only, not restricted to messages between licensed hams only, and there's no literal 1-minute duration cap or third-party-name logging requirement in either rule.

question: The frequency allocations of which ITU region apply to radio amateurs operating in North and South America?
explanation: The Americas (North and South) fall in ITU Region 2 under the international frequency-allocation framework that 97.301's band tables are built around; Region 1 covers Europe/Africa/the Middle East/former USSR, and Region 3 covers Asia-Pacific. 'Region 4' isn't a real ITU region at all - there are only three.

question: In what part of the 2.4 GHz band may an amateur station communicate with non-licensed Wi-Fi stations?
explanation: 97.111 authorizes amateur stations to communicate with other amateur stations plus a short, specific list of non-amateur exceptions (e.g. RACES/civil defense, telecommand of space stations) - an unlicensed Part 15 Wi-Fi access point or client doesn't fit any of those exceptions, so there is no part of the 2.4 GHz band where a ham may legally communicate with one, regardless of the fact the amateur 13cm allocation (2390-2450 MHz) numerically overlaps the low end of the Wi-Fi ISM band. That's why the answer is 'no part,' not a specific channel range.

question: What is the maximum PEP output allowed for spread spectrum transmissions?
explanation: 97.313(j) caps spread-spectrum (SS) transmitter output at 10 watts PEP - a much lower ceiling than the general 1500W HF limit, reflecting that SS's wide, low-power-spectral-density signal is meant to coexist with narrowband users rather than dominate the band. 100 milliwatts is far below the real limit, and 100W/1500W are both above it.

question: Why should an amateur operator normally avoid transmitting on 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz?
answers: A system of propagation beacon stations operates on those frequencies
A system of automatic digital stations operates on those frequencies
These frequencies are set aside for emergency operations
These frequencies are set aside for bulletins from the FCC
explanation: 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930, and 28.200 MHz are the operating frequencies of the internationally coordinated NCDXF/IARU International Beacon Project - roughly 18 beacon stations worldwide taking turns on a synchronized time-multiplexed schedule so hams can gauge real-time HF propagation. The specific frequency list itself isn't spelled out in the CFR text; the citation to 97.101 reflects the general 'good engineering and good amateur practice' duty to steer clear of a widely used, internationally coordinated resource like this rather than a numbered rule naming those exact frequencies.

question: On what bands may automatically controlled stations transmitting RTTY or data emissions communicate with other automatically controlled digital stations?
answers: On any band segment where digital operation is permitted
Anywhere in the non-phone segments of the 10-meter or shorter wavelength bands
Only in the non-phone Extra Class segments of the bands
Anywhere in the 6-meter or shorter wavelength bands, and in limited segments of some of the HF bands
explanation: 97.221 authorizes automatically controlled RTTY/data stations to communicate with other automatically controlled digital stations across the entire 6-meter-and-shorter bands, plus a short list of specific narrow HF sub-segments (the same eight windows referenced in G1B09/G1E03's rule) - not broadly 'any band segment where digital is permitted,' not restricted to Extra-only non-phone segments, and not the whole non-phone portion of every 10m-or-shorter band (HF auto-control access is much narrower than that).

question: When may third-party messages be transmitted via remote control?
answers: Under any circumstances in which third party messages are permitted by FCC rules
Under no circumstances except for emergencies
Only when the message is intended for licensed radio amateurs
Only when the message is intended for third parties in areas where licensing is controlled by the FCC
explanation: 97.115's third-party rules apply the same way whether the station is under remote control or locally operated - remote control by itself doesn't add or remove any restriction, so third-party messages may be sent by remote control under any circumstance where third-party traffic is otherwise permitted. The distinct restriction that does exist in this area applies to automatic control, not remote control - a different control category under which third-party traffic is barred except for RTTY/data emissions.

question: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on frequencies of 14 MHz or higher?
explanation: Above about 10 MHz -- 20, 17, 15, 12, and 10 meters -- upper sideband (USB) is the near-universal operating convention for SSB voice. There's no technical reason USB works better up there; it's just the convention every radio's factory default and every other operator's ear is built around, so straying from it just means nobody can understand you. "Suppressed sideband" and "double sideband" aren't sideband choices at all -- SSB by definition suppresses one sideband and the carrier no matter which sideband (upper or lower) you're using.

question: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter bands?
explanation: On 160, 75/80, and 40 meters -- all below 10 MHz -- the convention flips to lower sideband (LSB). This split at 10 MHz is purely a historical operating-practice line, not a rule or a technical requirement, but it's followed so universally that a station on the "wrong" sideband sounds garbled to everyone else on frequency.

question: Which mode is most commonly used for SSB voice communications in the VHF and UHF bands?
explanation: On VHF and UHF, SSB voice is always upper sideband, regardless of the LSB/USB-by-frequency convention that applies on HF. The 6-meter SSB calling frequency (50.125 MHz) and the 2-meter SSB/CW weak-signal segment (around 144.200 MHz) are both worked in USB only -- the HF convention of switching to LSB below 10 MHz doesn't carry over to VHF/UHF.

question: Which mode is most commonly used for voice communications on the 17- and 12-meter bands?
explanation: 17 meters (about 18 MHz) and 12 meters (about 24 MHz) are both well above the 10 MHz convention line, so like 20, 15, and 10 meters, SSB voice on these WARC bands is upper sideband by common practice.

question: Which mode of voice communication is most commonly used on the HF amateur bands?
explanation: Single sideband is by far the dominant voice mode across the HF amateur bands because it packs a voice signal into roughly half the bandwidth of double-sideband AM while putting all the transmitter's power into the intelligence-carrying sideband instead of wasting it on a carrier. FM is a VHF/UHF repeater mode (its wider deviation and capture effect don't suit crowded, weak-signal HF conditions), double sideband is essentially unused on amateur HF voice, and "single phase modulation" isn't a real mode.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of using single sideband, as compared to other analog voice modes on the HF amateur bands?
answers: Less subject to interference from atmospheric static crashes
Ease of tuning on receive and immunity to impulse noise
Less bandwidth used and greater power efficiency
explanation: Compared to double-sideband AM or FM, SSB's core advantage is efficiency: suppressing the carrier and one sideband cuts occupied bandwidth roughly in half and puts 100% of the transmitter's RF power into the sideband that actually carries the voice information, rather than wasting power on a carrier that conveys no information. It isn't higher fidelity (SSB actually sounds more compressed/narrower than AM or FM), it isn't inherently quieter in static crashes, and tuning SSB by ear is harder, not easier, than tuning FM or AM.

question: Which of the following statements is true of single sideband (SSB)?
answers: Only one sideband and the carrier are transmitted; the other sideband is suppressed
Only one sideband is transmitted; the other sideband and carrier are suppressed
SSB is the only voice mode authorized on the 20-, 15-, and 10-meter amateur bands
SSB is the only voice mode authorized on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter amateur bands
explanation: SSB is generated by taking a double-sideband AM signal and suppressing both the carrier and one of the two sidebands, leaving only a single sideband on the air -- so "only one sideband is transmitted; the other sideband and the carrier are suppressed" is the accurate technical description. The distractor about "one sideband and the carrier" describes a different (unused-in-ham-radio) hybrid scheme, and SSB is not legally the *only* voice mode on any of the bands mentioned -- AM and FM remain legal, just far less commonly used, on HF phone segments.

question: What is the recommended way to break into a phone contact?
answers: Say “QRZ” several times, followed by your call sign
Say “CQ” followed by the call sign of either station
explanation: The accepted way to break into an ongoing phone contact is to simply transmit your call sign once, during a natural pause, and wait to be acknowledged by the operators already talking. Repeating "QRZ" is what a station calling CQ or working a pileup says to invite callers, not what a caller says to break in; "Breaker breaker" is CB slang with no place in amateur practice; and sending "CQ" mid-QSO would incorrectly signal you're starting a fresh general call rather than asking to join an existing one.

question: Why do most amateur stations use lower sideband on the 160-, 75-, and 40-meter bands?
answers: Lower sideband is more efficient than upper sideband at these frequencies
Lower sideband is the only sideband legal on these frequency bands
Because it is fully compatible with an AM detector
It is commonly accepted amateur practice
explanation: There's no technical or regulatory reason LSB is used below 10 MHz -- both sidebands work equally well and both are legal on every phone band. It's simply longstanding, universally followed operating convention (much like driving on a particular side of the road), so following it is what lets other stations understand you without having to guess or manually flip sidebands. It has nothing to do with AM-detector compatibility -- a plain envelope AM detector can't cleanly demodulate SSB on either sideband without a product detector/BFO.

question: Which of the following statements is true of VOX operation versus PTT operation?
answers: The received signal is more natural sounding
explanation: VOX (voice-operated switch) keys the transmitter automatically whenever it detects your voice on the microphone, letting you operate hands-free without touching a push-to-talk button -- useful for mobile operation, digital-mode-adjacent voice work, or just convenience. It doesn't inherently make audio sound more natural (VOX can clip the first syllable if it's not tuned well, which PTT never does), doesn't reduce occupied bandwidth, and has no effect on transmitter power output.

question: Generally, who should respond to a station in the contiguous 48 states calling “CQ DX”?
answers: Any caller is welcome to respond
Any stations outside the lower 48 states
explanation: "CQ DX" from a station in the contiguous 48 states is a call specifically seeking distant/foreign contacts, so the courteous and expected response comes only from stations outside the lower 48 -- Alaska, Hawaii, US territories, and other countries all count as legitimate "DX" to a lower-48 caller. Answering a CQ DX from within the contiguous 48 states wastes the calling station's time chasing a contact they weren't looking for; the call has nothing to do with contests or with any single country like Germany.

question: What control is typically adjusted for proper ALC setting on a single sideband transceiver?
explanation: ALC (Automatic Level Control) is a feedback loop inside the transceiver that reduces RF gain when drive is too hot, to keep the transmitter's amplifier stages out of distortion/flat-topping. The one control an operator actually adjusts to set proper ALC action is transmit audio drive -- microphone gain (and any speech processor level) -- backing it off until the ALC meter shows only light, occasional activity rather than being pinned. Antenna reactance and attenuators affect the receive or antenna-matching side of the station, not how hard the mic is driving the transmitter.

question: Which of the following is true concerning access to frequencies?
answers: Except during emergencies, no amateur station has priority access to any frequency
Contest operations should yield to non-contest use of frequencies
explanation: 47 CFR 97.101(b) states that no frequency is assigned for the exclusive use of any station, and licensees/control operators must cooperate in selecting transmitting channels to make the most effective use of the spectrum; 97.101(c) then carves out exactly one priority rule -- control operators must give priority to stations handling genuine emergency communications (with a specific exception for RACES drills/tests, which get no such priority). Outside that emergency carve-out, no net, ongoing QSO, or contest operation gets to claim a frequency as "theirs" over anyone else -- which is exactly what makes answer C correct and the other three (each inventing a category of priority the rule doesn't grant) wrong.

question: What is the first thing you should do if you are communicating with another amateur station and hear a station in distress break in?
answers: Acknowledge the station in distress and determine what assistance may be needed
Immediately decrease power to avoid interfering with the station in distress
explanation: If a distress call breaks into your contact, the first move is to acknowledge the distressed station and find out what help they actually need -- that's the whole point of hearing the call, and delaying to notify a coordinator, cut power, or go silent first only slows down getting them assistance. Amateur radio's long-standing (and FCC-recognized, per 97.403's authorization to use whatever's necessary in a life-safety emergency) practice is that a station in genuine distress gets immediate attention from whoever hears it.

question: What is good amateur practice if propagation changes during a contact creating interference from other stations using the frequency?
answers: Advise the interfering stations that you are on the frequency and that you have priority
Decrease power and continue to transmit
Attempt to resolve the interference problem with the other stations in a mutually acceptable manner
explanation: When shifting propagation brings interference onto a frequency you're using, good amateur practice is to work it out cooperatively with the other stations involved -- since (per G2B01/97.101) no one has priority ownership of a frequency, "asserting priority" isn't a real option. Decreasing power while continuing to transmit doesn't actually resolve who gets the frequency, it just makes your own signal weaker while the conflict continues, and unilaterally jumping to the other sideband without coordinating doesn't resolve it either — it can just as easily create new interference of its own.

question: When selecting a CW transmitting frequency, what minimum separation from other stations should be used to minimize interference to stations on adjacent frequencies?
explanation: For CW, a minimum spacing of roughly 150 Hz to 500 Hz between signals is the accepted rule of thumb -- enough margin above a typical CW signal's actual occupied bandwidth (well under 150 Hz for the keyed tone itself) to account for receiver filter skirts, slight frequency drift, and the operator's own tuning precision, without needlessly hogging a wide chunk of a crowded CW subband. Much tighter spacing (5-50 Hz) invites overlap, and much wider (1 kHz+) wastes spectrum that dozens of other CW stations could be using.

question: When selecting an SSB transmitting frequency, what minimum separation should be used to minimize interference to stations on adjacent frequencies?
explanation: A voice SSB signal typically occupies around 2.4-3 kHz of bandwidth, so leaving 2 kHz to 3 kHz of separation between adjacent SSB transmitting frequencies keeps one station's sidebands from splattering into the next station's passband. Much tighter spacing guarantees overlap and mutual interference; the very wide 3-6 kHz figure over-allocates spectrum unnecessarily in a phone band that's often crowded.

question: How can you avoid harmful interference on an apparently clear frequency before calling CQ on CW or phone?
answers: Send “QRL?” on CW, followed by your call sign; or, if using phone, ask if the frequency is in use, followed by your call sign
Listen for 2 minutes before calling CQ
Send the letter “V” in Morse code several times and listen for a response, or say “test” several times and listen for a response
Send “QSY” on CW or if using phone, announce “the frequency is in use,” then give your call sign and listen for a response
explanation: Before calling CQ on an apparently clear frequency, the correct courtesy check is to ask if it's in use -- sending "QRL?" on CW, or asking "is this frequency in use?" on phone -- followed by your call sign, and then listening for a reply. This matters because you may not be able to hear one side of an ongoing contact (e.g., a weak or skip-only station the other party can hear that you can't), so silence on your end doesn't prove the frequency is actually clear. Sending "V"s, saying "test," or transmitting "QSY"/announcing the frequency in use are not the accepted courtesy signals for this purpose.

question: Which of the following complies with commonly accepted amateur practice when choosing a frequency on which to initiate a call?
answers: Listen on the frequency for at least two minutes to be sure it is clear
Identify your station by transmitting your call sign at least 3 times
explanation: Following the voluntary band plan -- the informally agreed-upon frequency allocations within each band for CW, digital, SSB, DX windows, and so on that amateurs maintain among themselves beyond the FCC's formal rules -- is the specific, real piece of accepted practice being tested here. The other choices state plausible-sounding but invented specifics (a fixed "2 minutes" of listening, or identifying "at least 3 times") that aren't actual requirements or documented norms, which is why "all these choices" is not correct even though listening first and identifying are both generally good habits.

question: What is the voluntary band plan restriction for US stations transmitting within the 48 contiguous states in the 50.1 MHz to 50.125 MHz band segment?
answers: Only contacts with stations not within the 48 contiguous states
Only contacts with other stations within the 48 contiguous states
explanation: The 50.1-50.125 MHz segment of 6 meters is the voluntary "DX window": by long-standing band-plan convention, US stations within the 48 contiguous states use this slice only to work stations outside the lower 48 (other countries, Alaska, Hawaii, etc.), keeping it clear for the weak, hard-to-work openings that DX contacts on 6 meters require rather than clogging it with routine in-country ragchews.

question: Who may be the control operator of an amateur station transmitting in RACES to assist relief operations during a disaster?
answers: Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license
Only a RACES net control operator
A person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license or an appropriate government official
Any control operator when normal communication systems are operational
explanation: Under 47 CFR 97.407(a), no person may be the control operator of a station transmitting in RACES unless that person holds an FCC-issued amateur operator license (the rule additionally requires the operator be certified as enrolled with the sponsoring civil defense organization, a detail this simplified answer choice omits but doesn't contradict). This rules out the other choices: RACES control isn't restricted to a formally designated "net control" operator, an unlicensed government official cannot legally be the control operator no matter their role in the disaster response, and RACES is specifically activated for civil-defense/disaster situations -- it isn't a status that applies to "any" control operator whenever normal communications happen to be up.

question: Which of the following is good amateur practice for net management?
answers: Always use multiple sets of phonetics during check-in
Have a backup frequency in case of interference or poor conditions
Transmit the full net roster at the beginning of every session
explanation: Good net management includes having a pre-arranged backup/alternate frequency ready in case interference, poor propagation, or a jammer knocks the primary net frequency out of usability -- it lets net control move the whole net without losing check-ins. Requiring multiple sets of phonetics or reading the full roster at the start of every session just burns net time without adding value; efficient net procedure trims exactly that kind of repetition.

question: How often may RACES training drills and tests be routinely conducted without special authorization?
answers: No more than 1 hour per month
No more than 2 hours per month
No more than 1 hour per week
No more than 2 hours per week
explanation: 47 CFR 97.407(d)(4) authorizes RACES training drills and tests as one of the permitted RACES communication categories, capped at no more than 1 hour per week routinely (with a separate, larger allowance of up to 72 hours twice a year when specifically approved by the sponsoring state/area civil defense organization). Exceeding that routine weekly hour without that special authorization isn't allowed under the rule.

question: Which of the following describes full break-in CW operation (QSK)?
answers: Breaking stations send the Morse code prosign “BK”
Automatic keyers, instead of hand keys, are used to send Morse code
An operator must activate a manual send/receive switch before and after every transmission
Transmitting stations can receive between code characters and elements
explanation: Full break-in CW (QSK) means the receiver is switched back on in the brief gaps between the dits, dahs, and spaces of your own keying, so you can actually hear if another station starts calling or breaking in while you're still sending -- true instant back-and-forth without ever touching a separate send/receive switch. Semi break-in (using a T/R relay that switches once per transmission, or manual switching) doesn't give you that between-element listening; sending "BK" or using an electronic keyer are unrelated features.

question: What should you do if a CW station sends “QRS?”
explanation: "QRS?" is the Q-signal asking "shall I send more slowly?" (or, stated as "QRS," an instruction/request to slow down), so the correct response is simply to send slower -- it has nothing to do with changing frequency, boosting power, or repeating content, all of which fail to address what the other operator is actually asking for: a copyable sending speed.

question: What does it mean when a CW operator sends “KN” at the end of a transmission?
answers: Listening only for a specific station or stations
explanation: "KN" at the end of a CW transmission means the sender is listening only for a specific station (or specific stations) to reply -- an exclusive invitation, as opposed to plain "K," which invites any station to respond. It doesn't mean no US stations should call, doesn't describe break-in operation, and doesn't mean the station is signing off (that's closer to "SK").

question: What does the Q signal “QRL?” mean?
answers: “Are you operating full break-in?” or “Can you operate full break-in?”
“Are you listening only for a specific station?”
“Are you busy?” or “Is this frequency in use?”
explanation: "QRL?" asks "is this frequency busy?" / "are you busy?" -- the standard courtesy check sent before calling CQ on an apparently clear frequency (see G2B06). It's unrelated to break-in operation (that's closer to a QSK-style question, not a standard Q-signal) and unrelated to "listening for a specific station," which is what "KN" signals instead.

question: What is the best speed to use when answering a CQ in Morse code?
answers: The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no slower than the CQ
The fastest speed at which you are comfortable copying, but no faster than the CQ
At the standard calling speed of 10 wpm
At the standard calling speed of 5 wpm
explanation: The guidance is to answer a CQ at the fastest speed you're comfortable copying, but capped at no faster than the CQ was sent -- since the calling station has only demonstrated they can send (and presumably copy) at that speed, going faster risks losing them, while there's no rule requiring you to slow all the way down to some fixed "standard" speed like 5 or 10 wpm if you and the other station can both comfortably go faster than that within the CQ's own pace.

question: What does the term “zero beat” mean in CW operation?
answers: Matching the speed of the transmitting station
Operating split to avoid interference on frequency
Matching the transmit frequency to the frequency of a received signal
explanation: "Zero beat" means tuning your own transmit frequency to exactly match the frequency of a signal you've received -- classically done by ear, listening for the audio beat note between your own sidetone and the other station's signal to drop to zero Hz difference. It's unrelated to matching sending speed, to split operation, or to sending without errors.

question: When sending CW, what does a “C” mean when added to the RST report?
answers: Report was read from an S meter rather than estimated
explanation: Appending a "C" to an RST signal report (an informal extension beyond the base Readability-Strength-Tone scale) flags a chirpy or unstable note -- typically a sign of power-supply sag or oscillator instability keying up and down with the code elements, common on some older or poorly-regulated transmitters. It's not a statement about copy accuracy, meter-based versus estimated reporting, or key clicks (which get their own separate informal notation, "K").

question: What prosign is sent to indicate the end of a formal message when using CW?
explanation: The prosign "AR" (sent as one run-together character, dit-dah-dit-dah-dit) marks the end of a formal message/transmission in CW traffic handling. "SK" ends the entire contact/QSO, "BK" signals a break for back-and-forth exchange, and "KN" invites a reply from one specific station only -- each is a distinct prosign with a distinct meaning, and only "AR" specifically closes out a formal message.

question: What does the Q signal “QSL” mean?
answers: We have already confirmed the contact
explanation: "QSL" means "I have received and understood" (as a statement) or "did you receive and understand?" (as a question, "QSL?") -- confirming successful copy of a transmission, which is also the basis for the paper/electronic "QSL card" tradition of confirming a contact after the fact. It doesn't mean "send slower" (that's QRS), and it isn't specifically about prior contact history (that's closer to informal chat, not a defined Q-signal).

question: What does the Q signal “QRN” mean?
explanation: "QRN" reports that the sender is troubled by (atmospheric) static -- natural noise from lightning and similar sources -- distinct from "QRM," which specifically means interference from other stations/transmissions. It has no connection to sending speed or to zero-beating a signal.

question: What does the Q signal “QRV” mean?
answers: There is interference on the frequency
I am quitting for the day
explanation: "QRV" means "I am ready" -- typically ready to receive, ready to proceed, or ready to copy traffic, depending on context. It's unrelated to sending speed, interference, or signing off for the day.

question: What is the Volunteer Monitor Program?
answers: Amateur volunteers who are formally enlisted to monitor the airwaves for rules violations
Amateur volunteers who conduct amateur licensing examinations
Amateur volunteers who conduct frequency coordination for amateur VHF repeaters
Amateur volunteers who use their station equipment to help civil defense organizations in times of emergency
explanation: The Volunteer Monitor Program is a network of amateur volunteers (coordinated jointly by ARRL and the FCC since it superseded the older Amateur Auxiliary/Official Observer program in 2016) who are formally enlisted to listen for, document, and report apparent rules violations on the amateur bands to the FCC. It's not the licensing-exam program (that's the separate Volunteer Examiner Coordinator/VE system), not a repeater frequency-coordination body, and not a civil-defense emergency-communications role (that's ARES/RACES).

question: Which of the following are objectives of the Volunteer Monitor Program?
answers: To conduct efficient and orderly amateur licensing examinations
To provide emergency and public safety communications
To coordinate repeaters for efficient and orderly spectrum usage
To encourage amateur radio operators to self-regulate and comply with the rules
explanation: A stated objective of the Volunteer Monitor Program is to encourage operators to self-regulate and voluntarily comply with the rules -- monitoring and gentle correction from fellow hams is meant to keep most rules issues from ever needing formal FCC enforcement action. It has no role in running license exams, providing emergency/public-safety communications, or coordinating repeater frequencies -- those are handled by entirely separate structures (VECs, ARES/RACES, and regional frequency coordinating bodies, respectively).

question: What procedure may be used by Volunteer Monitors to localize a station whose continuous carrier is holding a repeater on in their area?
answers: Compare vertical and horizontal signal strengths on the input frequency
Compare beam headings on the repeater input from their home locations with that of other Volunteer Monitors
Compare signal strengths between the input and output of the repeater
explanation: To localize a station whose stuck or continuous carrier is holding a repeater's input open, cooperating Volunteer Monitors in different locations each take a directional bearing (beam heading) toward the offending signal on the repeater's input frequency, then compare those bearings from their several home locations -- classic triangulation/direction-finding, the same principle used in a hidden-transmitter hunt. Comparing input-vs-output signal strength or vertical-vs-horizontal polarization at a single location doesn't localize a transmitter's position the way multiple cross-bearings do.

question: Which of the following describes an azimuthal projection map?
answers: A map that shows accurate land masses
A map that shows true bearings and distances from a specific location
A map that shows the angle at which an amateur satellite crosses the equator
A map that shows the number of degrees longitude that an amateur satellite appears to move westward at the equator with each orbit
explanation: An azimuthal projection map is centered on a single reference point (typically your own station) and is constructed so that the direction (bearing/azimuth) -- and often the distance -- from that center point to any other point on the map is shown accurately; that's exactly what a ham needs to point a directional HF antenna correctly toward a distant station. It's not chosen for accurate land-mass shape (that's what a Mercator or similar projection is for), and it has nothing to do with satellite orbital inclination or nodal westward drift, which are separate orbital-mechanics concepts entirely.

question: Which of the following indicates that you are looking for an HF contact with any station?
answers: Sign your call sign once, followed by the words “listening for a call” -- if no answer, change frequency and repeat
Say “QTC” followed by “this is” and your call sign -- if no answer, change frequency and repeat
Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” then your call sign a few times, then pause to listen, repeat as necessary
Transmit an unmodulated carried for approximately 10 seconds, followed by “this is” and your call sign, and pause to listen -- repeat as necessary
explanation: The standard way to call for any station on HF is to send "CQ" a few times, followed by "this is" (or "DE" on CW) and your own call sign a few times, then pause and listen for a reply -- repeating the cycle as needed. "Listening for a call" without a CQ, or a QTC-based call, or transmitting an unmodulated carrier before identifying, are not the accepted general-calling procedure.

question: How is a directional antenna pointed when making a “long-path” contact with another station?
answers: 180 degrees from the station’s short-path heading
explanation: A "long-path" contact means the signal is being worked around the far side of the globe rather than the shorter direct route, so the antenna must be pointed 180 degrees opposite the station's normal short-path (great-circle direct) heading -- essentially aiming away from the other station's actual direction to catch the propagation going the long way around. It has nothing to do with the sun's position, the gray line (a separate propagation phenomenon related to dawn/dusk enhancement, not to beam heading), or simply pointing north.

question: Which of the following are examples of the NATO Phonetic Alphabet?
explanation: "Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta" is the modern NATO/ICAO phonetic alphabet, standardized internationally and the one recommended for amateur use to spell call signs clearly over noisy or weak signals. "Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog" is the older US military/aviation alphabet retired in the 1950s, and the other two options aren't standardized phonetic alphabets at all.

question: Why do many amateurs keep a station log?
answers: The FCC requires a log of all international contacts
The FCC requires a log of all international third-party traffic
The log provides evidence of operation needed to renew a license without retest
To help with a reply if the FCC requests information about your station
explanation: Since the FCC no longer generally requires amateurs to keep station logs (that broad logging requirement was dropped decades ago, and today's Part 97 only mandates records in narrow cases like automatic control station identification), most hams who log do it voluntarily -- mainly so they have a documented, dated record to refer back to if the FCC ever asks about a specific transmission or contact from their station. It isn't tied to license renewal (which requires no operating evidence), and there's no FCC logging mandate specific to international contacts or third-party traffic today.

question: Which of the following is required when participating in a contest on HF frequencies?
answers: Submit a log to the contest sponsor
Send a QSL card to the stations worked, or QSL via Logbook of The World
Identify your station according to normal FCC regulations
explanation: The one thing genuinely required when contesting on HF is the same thing required in any other operation: identifying your station according to normal FCC rules (47 CFR 97.119, including the station ID interval). Submitting a log to the contest sponsor and exchanging/confirming QSL cards are common contest customs and often needed to claim an award, but they're rules of the contest, not FCC requirements -- which is why the correct answer is identification alone, not "all these choices."

question: What is QRP operation?
explanation: QRP operation refers to deliberately transmitting at low power -- conventionally 5 watts or less on CW/digital and around 10 watts or less on SSB, though the exam's answer keeps it general as "low-power transmit operation." It's a mode of operating philosophy/challenge (working long distances on minimal power), not a protocol, a model-aircraft control scheme, or a formal net procedure.

question: Why are signal reports typically exchanged at the beginning of an HF contact?
answers: To allow each station to operate according to conditions
To be sure the contact will count for award programs
To allow each station to calibrate their frequency display
explanation: Exchanging signal reports early in an HF contact lets each operator adjust how they're operating to the conditions being heard -- for example, slowing down CW speed, switching to phonetics, repeating information, or deciding whether a contact is even sustainable given a weak or noisy report. It isn't done to satisfy award-program bookkeeping, isn't part of formal radiogram/NTS message structure (which has its own separate preamble), and has nothing to do with calibrating a frequency display.

question: Which mode is normally used when sending RTTY signals via AFSK with an SSB transmitter?
explanation: By long-standing convention, AFSK RTTY sent through an SSB transmitter is run on lower sideband (LSB) -- a holdover from the days of mechanical teleprinters and dedicated RTTY terminal units, which standardized on LSB regardless of the usual HF LSB/USB-by-frequency convention (compare G2A01/G2A02, which is voice-only). USB, DSB, and CW are not the accepted convention for AFSK RTTY.

question: What is VARA?
answers: A low signal-to-noise digital mode used for EME (moonbounce)
A digital protocol used with Winlink
A radio direction finding system used on VHF and UHF
DX spotting system using a network of software defined radios
explanation: VARA is a modern software modem/protocol (VARA HF and VARA FM, developed by EA5HVK) most commonly used as the underlying ARQ data link for Winlink radio email, serving alongside (and in many setups replacing) PACTOR modems for that purpose. It isn't an EME weak-signal mode, a VHF/UHF direction-finding system, or a DX-spotting network -- those are unrelated technologies entirely.

question: What symptoms may result from other signals interfering with a PACTOR or VARA transmission?
answers: Failure to establish a connection between stations
explanation: PACTOR and VARA are both ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) protocols: when interference corrupts a data block, the receiving station automatically asks for a retransmission rather than passing along garbled data. That error-correction behavior means interference shows up not as garbled output but as visible protocol symptoms -- repeated retries/timeouts, long pauses while blocks are resent, or in bad enough conditions a total failure to link up at all -- so all three listed symptoms are genuine, real consequences of the same underlying retry mechanism.

question: Which of the following is good practice when choosing a transmitting frequency to answer a station calling CQ using FT8?
answers: Always call on the station’s frequency
Call on any frequency in the waterfall except the station’s frequency
Find a clear frequency during the same time slot as the calling station
Find a clear frequency during the alternate time slot to the calling station
explanation: FT8 (like the other WSJT-X modes) transmits and receives in strict, alternating ~15-second time slots -- a station calling CQ transmits in one slot and listens in the other, so to actually be heard by them, you need to transmit during the alternate slot from theirs, not the same one (transmitting in the same slot means you're both transmitting, and neither of you is listening for the other). Calling on their exact frequency is fine (FT8's decoder handles multiple simultaneous signals in the same slot), but the time-slot alignment is what actually determines whether a reply gets heard.

question: What is the standard sideband for JT65, JT9, FT4, or FT8 digital signal when using AFSK?
explanation: JT65, JT9, FT4, and FT8 -- all part of the WSJT-X digital-mode family -- are, by software and community convention, always operated on upper sideband (USB) when generated via AFSK, regardless of which HF band or frequency they're on. This overrides the older voice-mode LSB-below-10-MHz convention (G2A01/G2A02); digital-mode software and most rigs' data/USB presets are built around USB across the board.

question: What is the most common frequency shift for RTTY emissions in the amateur HF bands?
explanation: 170 Hz is the most common frequency shift used for amateur HF RTTY (the spacing between the "mark" and "space" audio/RF tones), matching the narrow-shift standard most amateur RTTY equipment and software defaults to, as opposed to the wider 425 Hz or 850 Hz shifts more typical of commercial/military RTTY services outside the amateur bands.

question: Which of the following is required when using FT8?
answers: Computer time accurate to within approximately 1 second
explanation: FT8 (and the other WSJT-X modes) rely on tightly synchronized 15-second transmit/receive time slots across both stations, so the software needs the computer's clock to be accurate to roughly within about 1 second (in practice, synced via NTP or a similar time service) or the decoder will be looking in the wrong part of the audio for a signal that's arrived early or late. It doesn't require special modem hardware (any standard sound card interface works), a specific receiver attenuator setting, or a particular antenna polarization.

question: In what segment of the 20-meter band are most digital mode operations commonly found?
answers: At the bottom of the slow-scan TV segment, near 14.230 MHz
At the top of the SSB phone segment, near 14.325 MHz
In the middle of the CW segment, near 14.100 MHz
explanation: On 20 meters, the digital-mode segment by band-plan convention runs roughly from 14.070 MHz to 14.100 MHz, sitting between the CW subband below it and the RTTY/data allocations and eventually the phone segment above -- this is where PSK31, RTTY, FT8, and similar modes are conventionally found, not down near the SSTV segment (~14.230 MHz) or up in the SSB phone segment (~14.325 MHz).

question: How do you join a contact between two stations using the PACTOR protocol?
answers: Send broadcast packets containing your call sign while in MONITOR mode
Transmit a steady carrier until the PACTOR protocol times out and disconnects
Joining an existing contact is not possible, PACTOR connections are limited to two stations
explanation: PACTOR is strictly a two-station, point-to-point ARQ link -- once two stations establish a connection, no third station can join in the way you might join a net or a packet BBS conversation; you simply cannot "break into" an active PACTOR session. Sending broadcast packets, a NAK code, or holding a carrier until timeout won't get you into someone else's link -- the protocol's design itself is exclusively two-party.

question: Which of the following is a way to establish contact with a digital messaging system gateway station?
answers: Send an email to the system control operator
Respond when the station broadcasts its SSID
Transmit a connect message on the station’s published frequency
explanation: To reach a digital messaging system gateway (such as a Winlink RMS station), you transmit a connect request on that gateway's published operating frequency -- gateways don't broadcast an SSID for you to "respond to," and there's no email- or Morse-based way to initiate the radio-side connection; the actual link is established over RF on the frequency the gateway operator has published for that purpose.

question: What is the primary purpose of an Amateur Radio Emergency Data Network (AREDN) mesh network?
answers: To provide FM repeater coverage in remote areas
To provide real time propagation data by monitoring amateur radio transmissions worldwide
To provide high-speed data services during an emergency or community event
To provide DX spotting reports to aid contesters and DXers
explanation: AREDN mesh networks exist primarily to provide high-speed IP data services -- self-forming, self-healing Wi-Fi-based mesh links on amateur microwave allocations -- for use during emergencies or community events where normal infrastructure is unavailable or overloaded. It has nothing to do with FM repeater coverage, monitoring transmissions to gather propagation data, or DX-spotting; those are unrelated to what a data mesh network actually does.

question: Which of the following describes Winlink?
answers: An amateur radio wireless network to send and receive email on the internet
A wireless network capable of both VHF and HF band operation
